column2: Overcoming here the luminous, he created the seven mental ones: the far-going, many-faring, prayerful, doubting mind.
The mind, urged by the wish to create, transforms creation; from it space arises, whose quality is held to be sound.
From space as it transforms arises the pure, mighty wind that carries all scents; its quality is held to be touch.
From wind as it transforms arises the element of light that dispels darkness, shining; its quality is called form.
From light as it transforms come the waters, made of taste; from the waters earth, whose quality is smell; this is called the first creation.
The qualities of each earlier pass to the later; as far as a thing reaches, so far it is held to have those qualities.
If some, through lack of skill, say that smell is found in water, they should know that it belongs to earth alone, and that water relies on wind.
These seven persons, each of different power, could not create beings separately without coming together on every side.
Coming together, relying on each other, they entered the support of a body; therefore he is called Purusha.
By dwelling in it the body is made, embodied and sixteenfold; the great elements enter it with action.
Having taken all beings for the practice of austerity, the first doer, the great being, they call Prajapati.
He indeed creates beings; he is the supreme Person; the unborn Brahma begets gods, sages, ancestors and men,
worlds, rivers, oceans, directions, mountains, trees, kinnaras, rakshasas, birds, beasts, deer and serpents, the imperishable and the perishable, both moving and unmoving.
Whatever deeds they took up in the earlier creation, those same they take up again and again as they are created.
Harmful and harmless, gentle and cruel, dharma and adharma, truth and untruth: whatever the Creator thinks, that pleases him.
The diversity in the great elements, in the objects of the senses and in forms, and the arrangement of beings, the Creator alone ordains.
Some who know action call human effort the cause; some brahmins say fate; others, thinkers on beings, say nature.
Human action, fate and nature are the three that bring fruit; some say these three are not distinct, lacking discernment.
This is so and is not so, "both," "neither": those who stand in action speak of what creates the world as uneven; those who stand in goodness see equally.
Austerity is the highest good of a creature; its root is self-control and calm; by it he obtains all desires he wishes in his mind.
By austerity one obtains that which creates the world; becoming that, he is lord of all beings.
Sages by austerity studied the Vedas day and night, the speech without beginning or end, eternal, put forth by the Self-born.
The names of the sages, and the creations in the Vedas, those born at the ends of nights: he gives those same to them.
Difference of names, austerity, action, the names of sacrifices and the accomplishments of the world; but the accomplishment of the self is said in the Vedas by ten steps.
What is said obscurely in the Vedic disputations is seen by the seers of the Veda; at the Vedanta ends it is shown clearly by the sequence of yoga.
This distinction born of action is joined with the pairs for the separated; but one who knows the accomplishment of the self mostly gives up strength.
Two Brahmans are to be known: the word-Brahman and the supreme; one skilled in the word-Brahman reaches the supreme Brahman.
For kshatriyas the sacrifices of undertaking, for vaishyas offering sacrifices, for shudras service sacrifices, and for the twice-born austerity sacrifices.
The rule of these sacrifices is in the Treta, not in the Krita; in the Dvapara sacrifices go to ruin, and likewise in the Kali.
Mortals of undivided dharma, seeing the Rik, Saman and Yajus separately for desired prosperity, practise austerity by austerities alone.
In the Treta all those mighty ones appeared together, restrainers of the unmoving and moving everywhere.
In the Treta these sacrifices and classes were united; in the Dvapara they are diminished by the restriction of life.
The Vedas are seen and not seen in the Kali, all of them; sacrifices perish with them, and only the bridges of dharma remain.
The dharma seen in the Krita age among brahmanas, established in the self-possessed, ascetic and learned,
is, age after age, joined with vows of adharma; the Vedic disputations, standing in their own dharma, are altered age by age.
As in the rains all beings are more numerous and are created in moving places, so the dharmas age after age.
As in the seasons the marks of the seasons are seen in manifold forms in turn, those same, so Brahma in days and nights.
The variety of time is ordained, without beginning or end, as told before; he gives birth to and devours the subjects.
He sets the place of origin, the restraint of beings, Yama; by nature they act, joined with many pairs.
Creation, time, action, the Vedas, the doer, the deed and the fruit of action: all this has been told you, son, that you asked me.
I shall tell the withdrawal, at the beginning of the night, when the day is gone, how the lord makes this universe the subtlest self.
In the sky seven suns burn with flame; by those flames all this world is filled and blazes."
[Vyasa said:] "Then, when all the unmoving and moving have dissolved, the earth is seen without wood or grass, like a tortoise's back.
When the waters take also the quality of earth, smell, then the earth, its smell taken, becomes fit for dissolution.
Then the waters stand, wavy and loud-sounding, filling all this, and standing and moving.
When light takes the qualities of the waters, dear, then the waters, their qualities taken, cease, and the lights.
When the flaming rays hide the sun standing in the midst, the whole sky is filled with rays and blazes.
When wind takes also the quality of light, form, then the light is quenched, and the great wind is shaken.
Then the wind, reaching its own root of origin, blows below, above, across, in the ten directions.
When space swallows the quality of wind, touch, then the wind is stilled, and space stands soundless.
Entering its quality, the moon swallows the mind; when the mind ceases, the self rests in the moon.
After a great time, intention brings him under its sway; intention swallows thought, and that is the highest knowledge.
Time swallows knowledge; scripture says Time is strength; Time swallows strength, but the learned one brings it under his control.
The learned one then brings the sound of space into himself; that unmanifest is the supreme Brahman, eternal and unsurpassed; so all beings have Brahman alone as their return.
This has been rightly told as it is, without doubt; it is to be understood as seen by yogis whose selves are supreme, made of knowledge.
Thus expansion and contraction of Brahman in the unmanifest occur again and again, at the beginning of the thousand ages, of the day and likewise of the night."
[Vyasa said:] "From birth rites on, a man's rites with their fees go on until his return home from the teacher who is a master of the Veda.
Having studied all the Vedas, devoted to serving his teacher, free of debt to his teachers, the knower of sacrifice should return home.
Permitted by his teacher, he should follow one of the four stages until the release of his body, according to rule:
by begetting offspring with a wife, or by celibacy, in the forest or in the teacher's presence, or by the dharma of the ascetic.
The householder is called the root of all four; in it the self-controlled whose passions are ripened succeeds everywhere.
With offspring, learned in the Veda, a sacrificer, freed from the three divine debts, afterward, purified, he goes by deeds to the other stages.
He should dwell at the most holy place on earth, a seat of learning; and strive there to reach eminence and excellent fame.
By great austerity, by crossing to the far shore of the sciences, by sacrifice, or by gifts to brahmanas, his fame grows.
For one dwelling in a house there is no other holy place than receiving, for gods, sages, ancestors, teachers, and the old, the weak and the hungry.
To those scorched in hiding and wishing to eat, he should give as he can, even more than is made, even beyond ability.
For the worthy and fitting there is nothing that should not be given; the good know that even the horse Uchchaihshravas should be brought.
So, appeased, Kavya of true pledge and great vow went to heaven, having saved a brahmana's life with his own life.
Rantideva and Sankritya, having given water to the great-souled Vasishtha, are honoured in the back of heaven, giving cold and hot.
Atreya, having given manifold wealth to the worthy Chandra and Damaya, the wise king, went to endless worlds.
Shibi Aushinara, having offered his limbs and his dear son of his body for a brahmana's sake, went from here to the back of heaven.
Pratardana, lord of Kashi, having given his own eyes to a brahmana, gains incomparable fame here and hereafter.
Devavridha, having given a divine umbrella with polished ribs, golden and of great splendour, went to heaven with his weapons.
Sankriti and Atreya, having taught the qualityless Brahman to their disciples, of great radiance, went to the highest worlds.
Ambarisha, the mighty, having given eleven hundred millions of cows to brahmanas, went to heaven with his weapons.
Savitri her two divine earrings, Janamejaya his body, having given up for a brahmana's sake, went to the highest world.
Vrishadarbhi gave all jewels, Yuvanashva dear women and a lovely dwelling, and reached that world.
Nimi of Videha gave his kingdom, Jamadagnya gave the earth to brahmanas, and Gaya gave the earth with cities.
When the rain did not fall, Vasishtha repeatedly revived all beings, as Prajapati the subjects.
Marutta, king and son of Karandhama, having given his daughter to Angiras, quickly went to heaven.
Brahmadatta of Panchala, best of the wise, a king, having given the treasure Shankha to the best of the twice-born, gained the worlds.
King Mitrasaha too, having given his dear Madayanti to the great-souled Vasishtha, went to heaven with her.
The royal sage Sahasrajit of great fame, having given up his dear life for a brahmana's sake, went to the highest worlds.
Shatadyumna, lord of the earth, having given a golden house filled with all desires to Mudgala, went to heaven.
The mighty king of Shalva, named Dyutiman, having given his kingdom to Richika, went to the highest worlds.
Madirashva the royal sage, having given his slender-waisted daughter to Hiranyahasta, went to the worlds praised by the gods.
Lomapada the royal sage, the lord, having given his daughter Shanta to Rishyashringa, was joined with abundant desires.
King Prasenajit of great splendour, having given a hundred thousand cows with calves, went to the highest worlds.
These and many others, great souls, of refined selves and master of their senses, went to heaven by giving and austerity.
Their fame is established as long as the earth stands; for by giving, sacrifice and creating offspring they gained heaven."
[Vyasa said:] "Those skilled in Vedic disputations and skilled in the self, who are good and greatly fortunate, see origin and dissolution.
So he should live by dharma and act as the refined do; a brahmin should seek livelihood without hindering beings.
One who has received knowledge from the good, refined, skilled in the shastras, doing his work in the world by his own dharma, true to his pledge,
the householder stands in these good deeds; that twice-born should always sacrifice with the five sacrifices, with faith.
Steadfast, careful, self-controlled, knower of dharma, self-possessed, free of joy, fear and anger, a brahmana does not fall.
Giving, study, sacrifice, austerity, modesty, honesty and self-control increase his energy and draw away sin.
With sin shaken off, wise, light of diet, master of his senses, having brought desire and anger under control, he should wish to lead himself to the seat of Brahman.
He should honour the fires and brahmanas, bow to the deities, and avoid harsh speech and violence joined with adharma.
What is full of anger, always greatly bewildered, the world is carried on by the great force seen in the rule, by the unobstructed power, by the current of nature.
By a great flood of Time, by whirlpools of rain, with waves of months, with the swiftness of the seasons, and with fortnights as reeds,
with the winking and opening of the eye as foam, with the speed of days and nights, with desire as the fearsome crocodile, with the Veda and sacrifices as boats,
with dharma as the island of beings, the sound of wealth and desire, truth as the steps on the shore, violence as the trees carried along,
in the midst of the lake of ages, with Brahman as its origin, beings made by the Creator are dragged to Yama's abode.
This the steadfast wise cross by rafts made of wisdom; those without rafts, being witless, what will they do?
What is fitting, the wise man crosses, not other folk; the wise man sees virtue and fault everywhere from afar.
The doubting, desire-natured, unsteady, of little mind, unwise, does not cross at all; he who stays does not go.
The raftless, carried along, meets great fault; for one seized by the crocodile of desire there is no raft of knowledge even.
Therefore the discerning should strive to emerge; this emerging of his is that he becomes a brahmana.
Born in a family clean on three sides, in triple doubt, doing triple deeds, he should therefore keep emerging and cross by wisdom.
For the refined, self-controlled, restrained, self-trained one, accomplishment follows directly, here and in the next world.
He lives in them as a householder, not angry or envious; he should sacrifice constantly with the five sacrifices, eating the remains.
He should live by the conduct of the good, act as the refined do, and seek a blameless livelihood without hindering dharma.
Knowing the truth of scripture and discernment, of refined conduct, wise, active by his own dharma, he too is unmixed by action.
Active, faithful, generous, wise, free of envy, knowing the difference between dharma and adharma, he crosses all that is hard to cross.
Steadfast, careful, self-controlled, knower of dharma, self-possessed, free of joy, fear and anger, a brahmana does not fall.
This is the earlier livelihood laid down for a brahmana; performing actions with knowledge, he succeeds everywhere.
The unwise, wishing for dharma, does adharma here, and does dharma that is like adharma, grieving as it were.
I do dharma, he says, and does adharma; and wishing for adharma he does dharma; the fool, not knowing both deeds, is born and dies as an embodied being."
[Vyasa said:] "The steadfast carry the unwise across on rafts built by wisdom; the unwise cannot carry others or themselves across at all.
The sage with faults cut off, joined by yoga, should practise the twelve and the ten, without fear of the means and ruin, of the results of action, pleasures and goals.
The wise, knowing conduct, by mind and by seeing, should restrain speech and mind by intellect, who wishes the highest knowledge; should restrain the self by knowledge, who wishes his own peace.
Even a very cruel person, if he follows these, whether a knower of all Vedas or one who knows no verses and does no muttering,
whether righteous and a sacrificer or the greatest sinner, whether a tiger among men or one held as impotent,
crosses the great difficulty, the ocean of old age and death. Thus, joining by this yoga even in the end, even one who merely wishes to know passes beyond the word-Brahman.
The lap is dharma, the covering modesty, the pole means and ruin, the axle apana, the yoke prana, the life wisdom, the bond the soul,
the nave consciousness, the beauty conduct, the rim grasping, touch and sight the carrying, the nose and ear the vehicle.
He who, silent, attains all seven concentrations, and the others behind and at the side, as many as are the main concentrations,
in order the earthy, the airy, space, water, the lordship of light, of ego, of intellect,
so too he gradually attains the lordship of the unmanifest; and he joins the powers of whoever has them, by yoga.
Then, for him joined by yoga and seeing success in the self, being churned, because of subtlety, he would show these forms.
As cold-season smoke subtly rests in the sky, so for one freed from the body the first form appears.
When the smoke ceases, the second form is seen, like the form of water in the sky; there he sees the self.
When the water passes, the form of fire shines; when that ceases, he sees a yellow-garment-like form, and his form appears of the colour of wool.
Then, reaching the white state, the unborn, subtle airy, the not-white subtlety of thought, the unmanifest of Brahman.
Hear also the fruits when these are born: for one born to the lordship of earth, creation is willed and ordained.
Like Prajapati, unshaken, he creates beings from his body, with a finger or thumb, or by hand and foot.
One quality of wind is said to shake the earth; becoming space, he vanishes in space because of sameness of colour.
By colour too he is grasped, and drinks from desire what is in the receptacle; his form is not seen by light, and likewise it is quenched.
When ego is conquered these five fall under his sway; when the good in the self and intellect are conquered he becomes master.
Then flawless insight comes to him wholly; and the manifest self reaches the unmanifest.
Hear from me at length the explanation of the unmanifest from which the world goes forth and is called manifest, and learn the enumeration made of the manifest.
The twenty-five principles are equal on both sides in yoga and in Sankhya; hear the differences there from me.
That is called manifest which is born and grows and decays and dies, joined with four marks.
The opposite of that is called unmanifest; two selves are also declared in the Vedas and the settled views.
Another born of four marks they call the fourfold group: the manifest, the born of the unmanifest, the awakened and the other, sattva and the knower of the field: these two are also shown.
There are two selves in the Vedas, and in those attached to objects; withdrawal from objects is the mark of success of the Sankhyas.
Without mine-ness, without ego, beyond the pairs, doubt cut, he is not angry, does not hate, and speaks no untrue word.
Abused or struck by a friend, he thinks no ill; he turns away from the three: speech, action and thought.
Equal toward all beings, he moves toward Brahman; he neither desires nor is averse, fixed in sustaining life only.
Not greedy, unpained, self-controlled, neither active nor inactive, his senses not scattered, his wishes not thrown wide, harming no beings: such a Sankhya is freed.
Now learn from me by what causes they are freed by yoga: one who has passed beyond the lordship of yoga is freed.
Thus has been told you this understanding born of states, without doubt; thus one becomes beyond the pairs and reaches Brahman."
[Shuka said:] "What is that knowledge, or the learning by which both are crossed, the dharma marked by action and that of withdrawal?"
[Vyasa said:] "He who by nature sees only non-being, without consciousness, flourishes again by wisdom, freed from cause, in all.
Those for whom own-nature alone is held to be the cause gain nothing, like those who thresh straw and husk.
Those of little mind who rely on this view, knowing nature as the cause, do not gain the good.
Nature is for destruction, a deed of delusion born of the mind; this is the explanation of the two, nature and power.
Farming and the like, the gathering of crops, vehicles, seats and houses were devised by the wise.
Of toys, houses, ailments and medicine, the wise are the speakers, and the knowers carry them out.
Wisdom joins with wealth, wisdom gains the good; kings enjoy kingdoms by wisdom, of like marks.
The high and low of beings are found by knowledge alone; for those created by learning, dear, learning is the highest goal.
The birth of all beings is of four kinds: womb-born, egg-born, sprout-born and sweat-born; one should observe it.
One should regard the moving as higher than the unmoving; for it is fitting that, of two compared, the one with activity is superior.
They say of the moving, two-footed and many-footed; two-footed ones, though many, are higher than many-footed.
They say of the two-footed, the earthly and the others; the earthly are higher, for they eat grain.
They say of the earthly, the middling and the best; the middling are higher, by their grasp of the dharma of their kind.
They say of the middling, those who know dharma and the others; those who know dharma are higher, by discerning what should and should not be done.
They say of those who know dharma, those who know the Veda and the others; knowers of the Veda are higher, for the Veda is established in them.
They say of knowers of the Veda, the speakers and the others; speakers are higher, grasping all dharma.
By them the Vedas are known with the fruit of the action of all dharmas, with sacrifices and entire; the Vedas came out from the speakers.
They say of the speakers, the knowers of the self and the others; knowers of the self are higher, by grasping birth and non-birth.
He who knows the two dharmas knows all; he knows all dharma; he is a renouncer of true intention, patient, and a lord.
The gods know as a brahmana him who is established in the knowledge of dharma, skilled in the word-Brahman and one who has settled the supreme.
Those who know what is within and without, over the sacrifice and over the deities, to them we bow; they are gods, dear, they are twice-born.
In them this whole being and the world with its peak is set; of their greatness there is nothing at all like it.
Having passed beyond the beginning, the end and action in every way, they are lords of the fourfold being, of all, self-born."
[Shuka said:] "If there were no such thing there, doubt would arise about the determination of action: is action nature, or knowledge, or again action?
[Vyasa said:] If here there is desire to know, if knowledge relates to the Person, I shall describe it by reasoning and perception; hear it.
Some men say human effort is the cause in actions; some praise fate; and others nature.
Human action, fate and nature are the three that bring fruit, separate; some do not discern this.
It is so and it is not so, "both," "neither": those established in action speak of unevenness; those established in goodness see equally.
In the Treta and Dvapara and those born of the Kali are full of doubts; in the Krita age, the ascetics are calm and abide in goodness.
All see without separateness in the Rik, Saman and Yajus; seeing desire and aversion separately, they practise austerity in the Krita.
Joined with dharma, ever given to austerity, of strict vows, by austerity he obtains all desires he wishes in his mind.
What is said obscurely in the Vedic discussions by seers of the Veda is shown clearly again in the Vedanta by the sequence of yoga.
For kshatriyas the sacrifices of undertaking, for vaishyas offering sacrifices, for shudras service sacrifices, and for the twice-born muttering sacrifices.
A twice-born with his work completed would be so through study; he may do other things or not; a friend of all is called a brahmana.
At the beginning of the Treta, all the Vedas, sacrifices and classes and stages are whole; in the Dvapara these are lessened by the restriction of life.
In the Dvapara the Vedas go to ruin, and so in the Kali; they are seen and not seen; at the end of the Kali, again and again.
Their own dharmas perish there, oppressed by adharma, and the juices of cows, earth, waters and herbs.
The Vedas are concealed by adharma, and the Vedic dharmas and stages; those who stand in their own dharma, the unmoving and moving, are altered.
As the rain rains on all earthly beings and creates limbs everywhere, so the Vedas age after age.
The variety of time is spread out, without beginning or end, as I told before, from which they come and go.
The Creator is the place of origin of beings, the restraint, Yama; by nature they act, created in many pairs.
Creation, time, steadiness, the Vedas, the doer, the deed and the fruit of action: this has been told to you, dear, that you asked me."
[Shuka said:] "With offspring, learned in the Veda, a sacrificer, aged, wise, free of envy: how does he reach the future, unattested Brahman?
By austerity, celibacy, total renunciation, intelligence, in Sankhya or in yoga: asked this, tell me.
By what means do men attain one-pointedness of mind and senses? You should explain that."
[Vyasa said:] "Not elsewhere than in knowledge and austerity, not elsewhere than in restraint of the senses, not elsewhere than in complete renunciation does anyone find success.
The great elements are all the first creation of the Self-born; mostly they are lodged in the bodies of living beings in the village."
Such a form had never been among women, Yudhishthira, as that of Duryodhana's daughter, fair of complexion.
By his virtues that lord of men brought all kings under his sway; having lived out his time and performed the sacrifices, he went to heaven in his body.
This earth, full of wealth and girdled by the sea, would give me no joy, bereft of you.
Seeing Gada lying down, filled with great anger, the bearer of the Sharnga bow, discus and mace then finished off all of them.
Hearing Narada's words, the righteous-souled king spoke, having addressed the gods and the kings of his side.
And Karna, the great archer, best of those who bear all weapons, has gone to the highest success, for which you grieve.
